[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.282] We hypothesized that higher categorical and temporal variability in IER strategy use would predict lower negative affect and higher positive affect compared to lower categorical and temporal variability.

For Aim 3, we investigated the association between day-to-day feedback and affect, in line with the description of feedback provided by Bonanno and Burton (2013). We assessed whether affect the previous day would moderate the association between change in IER strategy use and affect the subsequent day.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.329] We hypothesized that at higher levels of negative affect the day prior, greater change in IER strategy use from one day to the next would predict reduced negative affect. We also hypothesized that at lower levels of positive affect the day prior, greater change in IER strategy use from one day to the next would predict higher positive affect. However, given that it is unclear whether feedback influences already adaptive levels of affect, we did not make an a priori prediction regarding moderation effects of lower levels of negative affect or higher levels of positive affect the day prior.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.302] Aim 4 investigated the flexibility of emotion regulation conceptualized as the covariation of IER variability and environmental change (defined as the number of events experienced, a change in event type, or a change in the stressfulness of the event from one day to the next; Aldao et al., 2015). We predicted that higher covariation of IER variability and environmental change would predict lower negative affect and higher positive affect (see Table 1 and Figures S1-S4 in the online supplemental material  for an outline of the study hypotheses).

[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.414] The COVID-19 Pandemic

Participants for this study were recruited during the COVID-19 pandemic. The World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a global pandemic on March 11, 2020, and data collection for this study took place between April 20, 2020 and July 20, 2020. The pandemic was associated with many significant lifestyle changes: Physical distancing requirements were instated, and nonessential in-person businesses and schools were closed in many places worldwide.

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.446] Procedure

This study received approval from the University of British Columbia (UBC) Behavioural Research Ethics Board. After obtaining consent, participants completed the baseline questionnaire, which assessed demographic characteristics and other measures as part of the larger study. Participants who also consented to complete the daily diaries were sent the diaries through email at 5 p.m. each day for 14 days after the completion of the baseline questionnaire. Participants did not receive remuneration for their participation.
